work_baker_early.title: A day at the mill
work_baker_early.where: A house in the city, 201 BC

steps.say: There are no bakers' shops yet: the pistor pounds and grinds the grain for households. Your employer's slaves are at the war.

steps.timing: Pound the grain in the mortar, on the beat.

steps.line: He pays you in coin, and a loaf.

steps.end: Honest work for honest pay. He'll have you again.

steps.say: A donkey turns the millstone in the back, blindfolded so it won't get dizzy. You knead, load the oven, and stamp each loaf with the baker's mark.

steps.timing: Load the loaves and pull them out at the right moment.

steps.ask: The baker says: cut the dough a little short on each loaf. "Everyone does. The aedile's never here."

options.say: Eight loaves in a hundred are dough you never used. The baker grins.

steps.line: He pays you at the end of the day.

steps.end: You smell of the oven for two days. Half the Subura will eat what you made.

steps.say: The baker was born a baker and will die one: the law binds his family to the ovens, to bake the state's bread. His son ran off to be a priest and was brought back.

steps.ask: "Don't come back," he says quietly. "If you work here too long they'll put your name on the roll. Then you're a baker forever."

options.say: He looks at you as if you'd said you'd like to be buried alive.

steps.end: The state's bread is free for the people, and it costs the bakers everything.

steps.say: There is no flour. The mills on the river were smashed in the siege and the grain doesn't come. The oven is cold.

steps.end: The baker's family sits in the doorway. They have nothing to sell and nothing to do.

steps.say: Cloth is cleaned in vats of water and stale urine: the fuller collects it in pots at street corners. You tread the cloth all day, standing in it.

steps.timing: Tread the cloth in the vat, in rhythm with the man beside you.
steps.miss: You slip. He catches your arm.

steps.hold: Hang it over the sulphur frame to whiten it. Hold your breath.

steps.say: You've scorched the purple border of a senator's toga. The fuller goes white. He'll have to pay for it.

steps.line: He pays you, and tells you to wash.

steps.end: Nobody likes the smell of a fuller's. Everybody likes a clean toga.

steps.say: Cloth is cleaned in vats of water and stale urine: the fuller collects it in pots at street corners. You tread the cloth all day, standing in it.

steps.timing: Tread the cloth in the vat, in rhythm with the man beside you.
steps.miss: You slip. He catches your arm.

steps.hold: Hang it over the sulphur frame to whiten it. Hold your breath.

steps.say: You've scorched the purple border of a senator's toga. The fuller goes white. He'll have to pay for it.

steps.line: He pays you, and tells you to wash.

steps.end: The Emperor Vespasian taxed the urine they collect. When his son complained, he held a coin under his nose: "Does it smell?"

steps.say: The fuller cleans the soldiers' woollen cloaks before they march. Urine and water in the vat, and your feet.

steps.line: He pays you, and tells you the cloaks you trod will go to fight Pyrrhus.

steps.end: Clean cloaks for the legion. Even the fuller serves the Republic.

steps.say: A merchant needs a sack of grain taken from the Emporium up to a shop in the Subura. No map: "past the Circus, up the Vicus Tuscus, through the Forum, and up the Argiletum."

steps.pick: Which way is the Forum from the Circus Maximus?
steps.yes: Right: up the Vicus Tuscus between the Palatine and the Capitol.
steps.no: North: up the Vicus Tuscus. You find it, late.

steps.timing: Up the steps of the Argiletum with the sack on your shoulder: keep your balance.
steps.miss: You stagger. The sack nearly goes.

steps.line: The shopkeeper pays you at his door.

steps.end: Rome is carried on men's backs, up and down its hills, all day.

steps.say: The aqueducts run to the street fountains, not to the upper floors. A woman on the fifth floor needs two jars a day and can't carry them.

steps.timing: Fill the jars at the fountain spout without overflowing.

steps.hold: Up five flights of wooden stairs. Don't spill.

steps.line: She pays you in coins she keeps in a jar.

steps.end: The rich have water piped into their houses from the aqueducts. The poor have stairs.

steps.say: The aqueducts were cut in the first siege, eighteen years ago. The fountains are dry. Water comes up from the Tiber, brown.

steps.hold: Carry the jar up from the river.
steps.done: You set it down. It has sand in it.

steps.line: A family in a ruin pays you with a piece of bread.

steps.end: The fevers come with the river water. Everyone knows. There is no other water.

steps.say: The bookseller's slaves copy books by dictation, a dozen at a time. He needs another hand today.

steps.type: How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?

steps.ask: After hours, the bookseller brings out something else: Catullus's verses on Caesar and his friend Mamurra. Filthy, and very popular.

options.say: Caesar knows about them. He invited Catullus to dinner anyway.

steps.line: He pays you for the day.

steps.end: Rome reads everything: speeches, poems, scandal, the Senate's minutes posted on a board. Words move faster than soldiers.

steps.say: Near the Forum of Peace are the booksellers: the new Virgils, the new Martials, cheap copies for the provinces.

steps.type: Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with your power.

steps.line: He pays you, and says the provinces buy Virgil by the crate.

steps.end: Every schoolboy from Britain to Syria learns Virgil by heart. The poem of Rome is more Roman now than Rome.

steps.say: The Prefect Symmachus's plea to the Emperor, for the Altar of Victory, is being copied to send to friends.

steps.type: Not by one road alone can one reach so great a mystery.

steps.ask: A clerk from the bishop's household offers you money to copy something for him too: the bishop of Milan's reply.

options.say: You copy both. Symmachus's is better written. Ambrose's wins.
The clerk goes to someone else.

steps.end: The Altar stays out. The argument will be copied for a thousand years.

steps.say: A family wants an epitaph cut for their son, in the usual abbreviations. The mason draws the letters in red; you cut.

steps.pick: It begins with the letters D M. What do they stand for?
options: To the spirits of the dead (Dis Manibus)
steps.yes: D M: to the spirits of the dead.
steps.no: D M: Dis Manibus, to the spirits of the dead.

steps.pick: After his name: V A XIX. What is that?
options: He was a veteran of the 19th
steps.yes: Vixit annos: he lived nineteen years.
steps.no: Vixit annos XIX: he lived nineteen years.

steps.pick: At the end: S T T L.
options: May the earth lie light on you
steps.no: Sit tibi terra levis: may the earth lie light on you.

steps.done: The chips fly. The letters are clean.

steps.end: His name will be read by strangers for two thousand years. His parents paid for that.

steps.say: A freedman's family wants an epitaph, in the old plain style.

steps.pick: It ends H S E. What is that?
steps.yes: Hic situs est: here he lies.
steps.no: Hic situs est: here he lies.

steps.end: The freedman was a slave from Syria. On the stone he is a Roman citizen, forever.

steps.say: A Christian family wants their daughter's stone for the catacomb: a dove, and a few words.

options: S T T L: may the earth lie light
D M: to the spirits of the dead
steps.yes: In peace. The dead are not spirits below now; they are sleeping, waiting.
steps.no: In pace. The old formulas are for the old gods.

steps.hold: Cut the dove and the letters.
steps.done: The dove is a little crooked. They don't mind.

steps.end: The letters are worse cut than they were. There is more hope in them.

steps.say: There is no new marble. The mason cuts old stones smaller: a pagan epitaph turned over, a temple's cornice sawn into slabs.

steps.done: On the underside: D M, and a name, and XIX. Someone's son.

steps.end: Rome is being built out of Rome.

steps.say: The fishwife has more fish than she can sell before the noon heat turns them. "Take a basket to the steps and sell it."

steps.end: You bring her the money. She gives you a fish for yourself.
By noon they stink. She throws them to the dogs, and doesn't look at you.

steps.say: The boatman has hurt his hand. He needs someone to pole the ferry across with a family and their goat.

steps.timing: Push against the current. Keep her straight.
steps.miss: The current swings the bow round.

steps.line: The boatman pays you from the fares.

steps.end: The Tiber floods every few years, and every year takes someone.

steps.say: A man with a cup of four knucklebones. Dice are illegal except at the Saturnalia. Everyone plays.

steps.end: He pays you, with a look.
You pay him. He buys a round with it.

steps.say: Knucklebones for a cup of wine. No one's ever heard of a law against it; there's hardly anything to bet.

steps.end: He pours you the cup. "The Venus likes you."
You pour him the cup. He drinks to Mars and the legions.

steps.say: Dice are against the law. The aedile's men come round sometimes and fine the tavern keeper, who pays them to go away.

steps.end: You win. The man says you're lucky. He means something else.
You lose. Mark Antony, they say, gambled away a fortune and had a friend exiled for it pardoned.

steps.say: Everyone plays. The Emperor Claudius wrote a book on dice and had a board fixed in his carriage.
A board scratched into the stone: three rows of twelve. Five men each, three dice. A lone man hit goes back to the start.

steps.end: He sweeps up your coins and looks for the next man.

steps.say: A board of eight by eight, and glass counters: the soldiers' game. Shut an enemy in between two of yours and he's taken.

steps.end: "You've been a soldier," he says. "Or a lawyer."
"Too many legions, not enough general," he says, sweeping the board.

steps.say: Children play it on the pavement with pebbles, and so do bored guards: three stones each, three in a row.

steps.end: You win. The child demands another game.
You lose to a child. Everyone watching enjoys it.

steps.say: The money changer tests coins for merchants: rings them, weighs them, cuts them. He needs a second pair of eyes today.

steps.end: "You'll do," he says. "Keep one of the good ones. Know what you're holding."

steps.say: He lends at one in a hundred a month, which is the law, and more, which isn't. He knows where everyone lives.

options.say: He counts it out, and writes your name and your street.

steps.end: His slave walks you to the corner, and remembers your face.

steps.ask: "You owe me," he says. "With the interest."

options.say: "Time costs," he says, and writes a bigger number.

steps.end: Debt is older than Rome. The Twelve Tables let creditors cut a debtor's body in pieces. No one ever did. Probably.

steps.say: A man on the church steps with a bowl. One of his feet is gone.

steps.ask: He says the name of Christ and holds out the bowl.

options.say: He blesses you and your house.
He says the name of Christ to the next person.

steps.end: Alms are the Church's great teaching: the rich are saved by the poor. The poor stay poor.

steps.say: A charioteer of the Greens is short of a driver for a practice run in the morning: four horses, the full course.

steps.line: The Greens' trainer writes your name down.

steps.end: Charioteers are slaves and freedmen, and some are richer than senators.
They pick you up out of the sand. "Everyone goes over once," the charioteer says. "The ones who live learn."

steps.say: You ask the senator if he needs a man.

steps.end: He says: come to my house at dawn, with the others. That is how it's done.
